title: Blueberries and Cardiovascular Health: What a 28-Year Study in Women Reveals
metaDescription: A study analyzes the relationship between blueberry and anthocyanin intake and lipids and cardiovascular risk in women.
excerpt: A long-term analysis in the Women’s Health Study examines the impact of anthocyanins and blueberries on cardiovascular risk and blood lipids.
imageAlt: Fresh blueberries served in a ceramic bowl on a wooden table

blocks.text: Introduction: blueberry consumption and cardiovascular health

The relationship between diet and heart health is a subject of constant scientific research. In particular, the flavonoids known as anthocyanins, which give various fruits such as blueberries their characteristic pigment, have caught researchers’ attention because of their observed properties. Previous studies have suggested that these compounds and anthocyanin-rich fruits may have anti-inflammatory and blood-lipid-lowering effects. However, findings in the earlier medical literature on the direct association between the intake of these substances and the risk of cardiovascular disease have shown mixed results.

Understanding the real impact of including these foods in the diet over the long term requires a detailed analysis of large cohorts. For this reason, investigating whether there is a prospective relationship between anthocyanin or blueberry intake and major cardiovascular events, as well as their cross-sectional link with lipid levels and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP), is of great interest both to the medical community and to those who want to make informed decisions about their daily diet.
What the source says: findings in the Women’s Health Study

A recent publication based on data from the Women’s Health Study (WHS) evaluated the intake of total anthocyanins, six subclasses of anthocyanins and blueberries. The research analyzed information from 38,088 women who completed a semi-quantitative food frequency questionnaire between 1992 and 1995. The scientists calculated multivariable hazard ratios (HR) for confirmed major cardiovascular events, a category that included non-fatal myocardial infarction, non-fatal stroke and death from cardiovascular disease.

During a follow-up period with a median of 28.0 years, a total of 2,752 cases of major cardiovascular events were recorded. In the initial analyses adjusted only for age, energy and WHS study treatment, hazard ratios across quintiles of total anthocyanin intake were 1.00 for the reference first quintile, 0.87 for the second quintile (95% CI: 0.78–0.98), 0.79 for the third (95% CI: 0.70–0.89), 0.81 for the fourth (95% CI: 0.72–0.91) and 0.88 for the fifth quintile (95% CI: 0.79–0.99), with a P trend of 0.23.

However, when a fuller multivariable adjustment was made that included additional clinical, lifestyle and dietary factors, the researchers observed that no statistically significant associations persisted with the risk of major cardiovascular events or their individual components. Similar null findings were identified when analyzing the anthocyanin subclasses and blueberry intake separately.

On the other hand, the research included a cross-sectional analysis in a subgroup of 26,912 women who provided blood samples at the start of the study. In this group, multivariable odds ratios were calculated for adverse levels of lipids and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP). The results showed that higher intake of total anthocyanins and their subclasses (except pelargonidin) was significantly associated with a lower probability of adverse levels of high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol and triglycerides, reaching a P trend below 0.05 in those cross-sectional analyses.
Context: comparison with what was known about blueberries

Previous scientific literature had already shown that anthocyanins and berries rich in these pigments have lipid-regulating effects and anti-inflammatory properties in various test settings. However, the evidence on whether this translates into a direct, prospective reduction in cardiovascular events in the population remained contradictory.

This study brings clarity by distinguishing between cross-sectional findings and very long-term prospective follow-up. While the cross-sectional data from the subgroup with blood samples support the hypothesis that higher anthocyanin intake is favorably related to specific lipid markers such as HDL cholesterol and triglycerides, the evidence from the 28-year follow-up indicates that, after adjusting for the full set of lifestyle, clinical health and other dietary factors, intake did not show a statistically significant association with a reduction in serious cardiovascular episodes.
What it means for you: practical application and moderation

For the consumer, these findings offer a balanced perspective on the role of anthocyanin-rich fruits such as blueberries within the eating pattern. The observed associations with more favorable HDL cholesterol and triglyceride profiles suggest that including these fruits is part of habits that go along with better metabolic indicators.

However, it is essential to avoid hasty conclusions or attributing miraculous qualities to a single food. The data show that eating blueberries alone does not guarantee absolute or prospective protection against heart attacks or strokes, since overall cardiovascular risk is shaped by a complex network of clinical and lifestyle factors. Including a variety of fruits should be understood as one component within a healthy lifestyle and not as a single solution.
Conclusion: balance of the scientific evidence

The long-term analysis of the Women’s Health Study concludes that anthocyanin and blueberry intake did not show a significant prospective association with the risk of major cardiovascular events after thorough adjustment for variables. However, the cross-sectional analyses confirmed a lower probability of adverse HDL cholesterol and triglyceride levels in women with higher anthocyanin intake.
